accepted.question_text: Let T be a rooted labelled tree with n parking spaces and let f be an n-mapping on [n]. For m drivers, write S(T, m) for the number of parking sequences that successfully park on T and S(f, m) for the analogous number for f. Is there a simple general characterization of the counting functions S(T, m) and S(f, m), rather than only case-by-case formulas or bounds?

evidence.quote: (1) Given a tree T or a mapping f, is it possible in general to give some simple characterization of the numbers S(T, m) and S(f, m), respectively?

accepted.question_text: Can the methods used to count parking functions on random trees be extended to determine the total number of parking functions for other important labelled tree families, such as labelled binary trees and labelled ordered trees?

evidence.quote: (2) With the approach presented, one can also study the total number of parking functions for other important tree families as, e.g., labelled binary trees or labelled ordered trees.

accepted.question_text: For increasing and decreasing tree families, especially recursive trees viewed as unordered increasing trees, can one determine the total number of parking functions or related aggregate quantities such as sums of parking functions, despite the fact that the differential equations produced by the current approach do not appear to have tractable solutions?

evidence.quote: (3) The problem of determining the total number of parking functions seems to be interesting for so-called increasing (or decreasing) tree families. For so-called recursive trees, i.e., unordered increasing trees, the approach presented could be applied, but the differential equations occurring do not seem to yield tractable solutions. For such tree families quantities such as the sums of parking functions as studied could be worthwhile treating as well.

accepted.question_text: For tree parking functions and mapping parking functions, what can be proved about displacement statistics, including the total displacement of all drivers and the individual displacement of the k-th driver, where displacement means the driving distance from a driver's preferred parking space to the space where that driver actually parks?

evidence.quote: (4) As for ordinary parking functions one could analyse important quantities for tree and mapping parking functions. E.g., the so-called total displacement (which is of particular interest in problems related to hashing algorithms), i.e., the total driving distance of the drivers, or individual displacements (the driving distance of the k-th driver) seem to lead to interesting questions.

accepted.question_text: For trees T and mappings f with parking sequence s, can one enumerate or otherwise analyze defective parking functions, meaning pairs (T, s) or (f, s) in which exactly k drivers fail to park successfully?

evidence.quote: (5) A refinement of parking functions can be obtained by studying what has been called defective parking functions or overflow, i.e., pairs (T, s) or (f, s), such that exactly k drivers are unsuccessful. Preliminary studies indicate that the approach presented is suitable to obtain results in this direction as well.

accepted.question_text: Can one solve enumeration problems for restricted classes of parking functions on rooted trees or on mappings, rather than only for the unrestricted parking functions considered in the existing counting results?

evidence.quote: (6) One could consider enumeration problems for some restricted parking functions for trees (or mappings).

accepted.question_text: Let X_n be the random variable equal to the number of parking sequences with n drivers that succeed on a uniformly chosen labelled unordered tree T of size n. Beyond the known first-moment asymptotic E(X_n) = F_n / T_n, can one determine higher moments of X_n or obtain nontrivial information about the full distribution of X_n?

evidence.quote: (7) Let us denote by Xn the random variable measuring the number of parking functions s with n drivers for a randomly chosen labelled unordered tree T of size n. Then, due to our previous results, we get the expected value of Xn via E(Xn) = Fn/Tn ... However, with the approach presented here, it seems that we are not able to obtain higher moments or other results on the distribution of Xn.

accepted.question_text: Suppose one studies parking on trees or connected components formed by parked cars when either the offspring distribution of the underlying random tree or the distributions of car arrivals have infinite third moment and tail behavior of the form c * k^{-gamma} for some constant c and gamma in (3, 4). Whether one looks at strongly connected or weakly connected components, is the critical component size of order n^{(gamma-2)/(gamma-1)}?

evidence.quote: In the above paper, Contat conjectures that no matter if one considers strongly or weakly connected components, when the offspring distribution of the tree or the car arrivals distributions have an infinite third moments and a tail of order c • k^{-gamma} for some constant c and some gamma in (3, 4) when k goes to infinity, the size of the components should be of order n^{(gamma-2)/(gamma-1)} at criticality.

accepted.question_text: For parking problems on random trees, especially in regimes involving heavy-tailed car-arrival distributions and frozen modifications of the Erdos-Renyi process, can one prove scaling-limit results in Gromov-weak or Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov type metric topologies, and do the resulting limits relate to additive and multiplicative coalescents or to inhomogeneous continuum random trees?

evidence.quote: At present, issues of studying parking problems in different metric topologies remains largely unaddressed. Contat and Curien (2023) have themselves pointed to appropriate contributions to follow in this sense ... It seems as expected that scaling limit results, in particular when combined with frozen modification of the Erdos-Renyi process would combine additive and multiplicative coalescent, due to the connection with Gromov-weak and Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov topologies. Limiting results could relate to inhomogenous continuum random trees as described in Bhamidi, van der Hofstad and Sen (2018).

accepted.question_text: When parking problems on random trees are extended to metric-topology settings, are dimensions 3 and 4 distinguished or critical in an analogous way to the role that these dimensions play in several other probabilistic models?

evidence.quote: Dimensionality issues have remained unaddressed in this line of research and one would be tempted to ask if dimensions 3 and 4 would be special also for this probabilistic problem, similar as they have proven to be in several other cases in probability theory (Hutchcroft, 2025).

needs_review.question_text_raw: Additional possibilities for research could also be found in extensions of the frozen modification of the Erdos-Renyi process, or even other random graph possibilities, such as preferential attachment models. Connections to present line of research in network archaeology would be interesting to explore. Finally, connections to other present probability and stochastic process research strands, in particular interacting particle systems or even random matrix theory provide an at present blank field of research.
